title: Better than anyone expected
problem: The task was to add a small animation to the home page without any designs.
solution: I significantly improved the animation, added interaction, and optimized it with lazy loading and animation-level performance work. It ran smoothly even on older phones. I also introduced a symbolic reward for interacting with it. Although the product was not related to entertainment, the mini-game attracted many daily users and increased product engagement. Management and marketing built a summer campaign around this unexpected success, with many bloggers taking part. I turned a small animation into the summer's killer feature with millions of engaged users.
context: Summer 2024 campaign · a product with millions of users

title: One person against a huge project
problem: One of three frontend developers moved to another team and another went on extended leave. The managers brought in a large project with a very tight deadline.

I learned the unfamiliar tools while working part-time and delivered the project alone by the deadline. The resulting Rive example and reusable component became the foundation for future Rive integrations across the team and Yandex Plus.

title: Tested a new stack with a game
problem: For new projects at MTS we had to decide whether Svelte + Threlte + Pixi.js was the right stack: could it handle 3D, 2D effects and UI in one app, and how fast could we build with it.
solution: To test the stack on a real task rather than a demo, I built Alchemy Terrarium in 4 days: a browser 3D game where you gather mushrooms in a forest and brew potions from them in a cauldron in a greenhouse. The 3D scenes run on Threlte (three.js), particle effects on Pixi.js on top of the 3D, the UI and game state on Svelte 5 — all in TypeScript and SvelteKit with a static build. The stack proved itself and was adopted for new projects. Later I compressed the game's 3D models with gltf-transform and meshopt: it now loads 9.7 MB on start instead of 76.4 MB.
context: May 2026, my first month at MTS. Model weight after compression in October 2026, gzip
facts: Learned the stack on the go

title: This website
problem: A portfolio of a developer whose main argument is performance. The site itself has to be the proof: 3D, animations, and interactivity — while still flying on any phone.
solution: The site was rewritten from React to SvelteKit with prerendering: every page is ready-made HTML, and the first screen ships only the JS it needs. The Threlte prism and Pixi scenes load after the page and render frames only while animating, then fall asleep at rest. The metrics in “Why me” are live measurements in the visitor's browser via the Performance API. A service worker makes the site a PWA and caches only what the visitor has already downloaded.
facts: GitHub Pages and my own metrics service in Go

title: My own language: JavaScript on every core
problem: JavaScript runs on one thread: a heavy computation takes one core and blocks everything else, while Web Workers need separate files, postMessage and copying data by hand. I wanted to write parallel code as simply as in Go — with strict types and without paying for the convenience in the bundle.
solution: I built Rook, a language with JavaScript semantics, Go syntax and static types, focused on speed and concurrency. go f(x) runs a function as a goroutine in a pool of Web Workers or worker threads, one thread per core, and gives a Promise of the result; channels, select, after and tick work as in Go. go for is the same loop over an array, one word longer: the array is split into parts, several per core, and each runs on the first free core. On the 14 cores of an Apple M4 Pro such a loop is 8.1 times faster than one thread. The compiler moves the function and everything it uses into the worker by itself and checks before the program runs that what goes to another thread can be copied there: a function, a class instance or a DOM element cannot be sent. The compiler is written in TypeScript: a lexer, a parser and a type checker with generics, union types, null safety and narrowing. It reads the types of npm packages and the DOM from .d.ts files and writes .d.ts files for Rook modules, so the language works with any npm library in both directions. Code compiles to readable JavaScript with a small runtime for channels and goroutines, imported by name; components compile to direct DOM calls, with no virtual DOM. Around the language there is the rooklang npm package, a CLI, a Vite plugin, a VS Code extension and documentation written in Rook itself, with a playground right in the browser.
context: Numbers from the repository: go for as measured on the docs home page, goroutines from the docs example in Node; both on a 14-core Apple M4 Pro
